name: Private Equity
summary: Equity in companies that are not publicly traded, held through closed-end buyout and venture funds that draw committed capital via capital calls over several years and return it through distributions. It is the growth sleeve of an alternatives program, and the decision turns on one question: can the investor fund its spending and those capital calls from liquid assets through a downturn long enough for the illiquidity premium to pay.

pros.text: The growth allocation. Private equity, buyout and venture, targets equity-like or higher long-run returns, in part by harvesting an illiquidity premium and manager skill that public markets do not offer. In the four-role framework it fills growth, not income, not diversification and not inflation protection.

For a long-horizon investor, tolerating illiquidity creates an opportunity to improve expected return and diversification and to access a broader strategy set, and in mean-variance terms adding illiquid assets to the eligible universe may shift the efficient frontier upward, more return per unit of risk. Keep it an opportunity rather than a result: realizing it depends on access and manager selection, and de-smoothing removes much of the apparent diversification gain. Deliberate illiquidity is the return source, so liquidity planning exists to survive it, not to eliminate it.

The quantitative case can be made with the case numbers: the proposal that raises private equity from 18% to 23% (alongside real assets 13% to 16%, funded from public equity and fixed income) carries an expected nominal return of 7.8% against 7.5%, volatility of 13.2% against 12.5%, Sharpe 0.34 against 0.33, and over 20 years at 5% spending a 30% against 35% probability of losing a quarter of purchasing power. A modest volatility increase buys better long-run purchasing-power preservation, and the proposed 13.2% still sits inside the board's 12% to 14% long-term volatility range. Those figures belong to the whole proposed allocation, not to the private equity leg alone.

Private equity lowers the risk of missing a long-term real return target relative to an allocation heavy in investment-grade fixed income. Investment-grade fixed income's lower expected return may simply not reach the real spending target, and the case assigns it a lower expected Sharpe ratio, which is the structural argument for holding less of it. This is the direction not to reverse: shortfall risk is higher for the fixed-income-heavy allocation, not for the private equity one.

cons.text: Illiquid exactly when liquidity is needed. Multi-year lock-ups, capital calls that can exceed distributions in a down market, and secondary sales that are costly, slow and priced at a discount, so this is not the asset a drawdown is funded from. In practice an illiquid allocation is rebalanced through the commitment and reinvestment pacing channel rather than by selling.

It diversifies equity risk only weakly. Private equity still carries equity beta, so its potential to diversify public equity is moderate, materially weaker than the strong diversification potential of the investment-grade fixed income it would replace, which is exactly why that substitution raises portfolio volatility. A portfolio of high yield, public equity and private equity loads heavily on one equity and credit factor and the three fall together, so the diversification across those labels is largely illusory. The illiquidity-premium argument for a broader opportunity set is a separate claim from hedging equity risk; do not run the two together, and do not write that private equity has no diversification value at all.

Reported risk is understated. Appraisal-based valuations are infrequent and lag the market, so returns are positively autocorrelated, which dampens measured volatility and lowers measured correlation with public assets. The curriculum's illustration is a private real-asset fund reporting about 8% volatility that de-smooths to roughly 12% to 13% with a higher equity correlation, so take it as the direction and rough size of the adjustment rather than as a private equity number.

Fees are high and performance-based, so net return is far below gross, and an alternative must never be judged on a gross return. The curriculum's 2 and 20 arithmetic is a hedge-fund illustration: on a 10% gross return, a 2% management fee plus 20% of the 8% above it nets 6.4%, a 3.6% drag, about 36% of the gross return. Carry that across as the size of the drag on an alternatives fee stack, not as a private equity calculation, because buyout and venture carry runs on realized proceeds above a preferred return with a catch-up and clawback while the management fee sits on committed capital. The gradable point is that the drag is large, which is why private equity and private real estate are modelled on net-of-fee return assumptions.

Manager selection drives the outcome and there is no exit from a bad one. The gap between top-quartile and bottom-quartile managers is far wider than in public markets, and because a disappointing private fund cannot simply be sold, monitoring has to do the work that selling does elsewhere: manager and organizational change, key-person departures and style drift, valuation practice, leverage and counterparty risk, and actual against planned calls and distributions.

The J-curve. Early years show negative net cash flow and negative reported returns because fees and capital calls precede realizations, and committed capital is not invested capital. Spending has to be funded from elsewhere through those years.

whenToRecommend: A perpetual or multi-decade horizon with modest near-term liquidity needs, a professional investment staff and scale: a large endowment or a sovereign savings fund is the investor that can safely harvest the illiquidity premium.

Forward return expectations are low across every asset class, fixed income carries a lower expected Sharpe ratio which warrants holding less of it, and the investor still has to hit a real spending target. Argue the case structurally, lower expected returns everywhere, a portfolio more conservative than peers', a lower fixed-income Sharpe and Monte Carlo evidence on the target, not as market timing and not as peer conformity.

The existing private program is mature: two decades of gradual build-up, diversified across managers, strategies and vintage years, with established access. That supports going further, where a new concentrated program would not.

The role the portfolio needs filling is growth. Match role to category: private equity for growth, core real estate or private credit for income, macro or market-neutral or trend for diversification, real assets for inflation.

A very large fund facing capacity limits and market impact in small or niche classes, which is pushed toward liquid large-cap holdings but can access scale-only strategies such as large private equity and direct real estate.

The liquidity budget and stress tests confirm that liquid assets can still meet spending and capital calls together in a high-stress state, with the minimum time-to-cash target intact. State the recommendation as conditional on risk tolerance and the liquidity budget, never on the claim that liquidity is not a concern.
whenNotTo: The investor has near-term liabilities, large scheduled withdrawals or a short horizon, so it cannot safely harvest the illiquidity premium. Keep the liquid allocation, or use liquid alternative substitutes.

The stated need is an equity-risk mitigator or something that holds up when equities fall. Private equity keeps equity beta and cannot be sold mid-crisis. Use high-quality government bonds for the reliable liquid hedge, noting that the negative-correlation cushion weakens at low yields. Trend and managed futures earn crisis alpha at a higher expected return than bonds, but the hedge is less certain and strategy-dependent and those vehicles often carry lock-ups of their own, so they belong in the allocation as a return-generating diversifier, not as the liquid cushion the IPS is asking for.

A small pool blocked by high minimums, with no dedicated staff and no way to diversify across managers and vintages. Recommend a smaller allocation or liquid alternatives, not the full illiquid program.
The investor is reaching for private markets during stress to fix a liquidity problem. Adding illiquid exposure in stress is the problem, never a tool.
Spending has to be funded from contractual current income. Private equity distributions arrive on the GP's schedule. Core real estate, infrastructure or private credit are the income categories.

An unconstrained single-period mean-variance optimizer is being run on raw appraisal-based inputs. Reject the weight it produces: de-smooth or constrain the inputs, or move to Monte Carlo or a risk-factor allocation.
pitfalls: Calling private equity a diversifier of equity risk. Under a risk-factor lens it is largely the equity factor the portfolio already owns, so its potential to diversify public equity is moderate at best. Name the shared factor rather than noting that correlation is below one.

Treating reported volatility and correlation as measured facts. Stale valuations understate both, in the same direction. A claim that private equity's correlation with public equity is measured more accurately than public fixed income's is wrong: the public series comes from continuous market prices.

Comparing a fund's reported IRR with a public manager's return. IRR is money-weighted and sensitive to the timing of calls and distributions, and appraisal lags flatter interim figures. Use PME or vintage-peer benchmarks. Under GIPS, money-weighted returns are permitted where the firm controls the external cash flows and the portfolio is closed-end, fixed-life, fixed-commitment, or significantly invested in illiquid assets, which is why private equity and real estate qualify. Illiquidity is one trigger among those, not a second necessary condition.

Forgetting the denominator effect. 800 public and 200 private is a 20% private share against a 25% limit. Public falls 30% to 560, the private mark stays near 200, and the share is 200 / 760 = 26.3%, through the limit with no transaction at all.

Rebalancing private equity like a public class. In practice an illiquid allocation moves through the commitment and reinvestment pacing channel rather than by selling, because secondary sales are costly and slow. Corridor widths in the case are set by both liquidity and volatility, which is why private equity gets the widest: 23% plus or minus 5%, so 18% to 28%, against plus or minus 3% for fixed income and plus or minus 2.5% for domestic equity. So do not rank corridor width by illiquidity alone, and do not propose a secondary sale to cure a corridor breach.

Quoting a value-at-risk number for the private book as though it settled the risk question. Its inputs are appraisal-based and its distributional assumption understates the tail, so pair it with conditional value-at-risk, the expected loss beyond the threshold, and with scenario and stress analysis.

cues.signal: The portfolio holds high yield, public equities and private equity, and is described as well diversified across three asset classes.
cues.implication: The diversification is largely illusory. All three load on the same equity and credit factor and fall together in a downturn. Answer with a factor decomposition, not with asset-class labels.

cues.signal: Private equity's reported volatility looks low and its reported correlation with public equity looks modest.
cues.implication: Appraisal smoothing. Lagged marks create positive autocorrelation, which dampens measured volatility and correlation. De-smooth before any optimization or risk comparison, and expect both numbers to rise: correlations reported in the 0.3 to 0.5 range may be nearer 0.7 to 0.8 once de-smoothed.

cues.signal: An unconstrained MVO run assigns a large weight to private equity.
cues.implication: The inputs are the error, not the optimizer. Returns are non-normal and path-dependent through calls and lock-ups, and the risk inputs are smoothed. Fix with de-smoothed or constrained inputs, Monte Carlo, or a factor-based allocation.

cues.signal: Public equities fall sharply, the private marks have not moved, and the IPS carries a private-asset limit.
cues.implication: Denominator effect. The private share breaches the limit without a single trade. Do not recommend a discounted secondary sale: slow new commitments, and state that liquidity planning should have anticipated this.

cues.signal: The IPS asks for a risk mitigator against the long equity position, or for an asset that works when equities drop.
cues.implication: Rules private equity out on both tests: it is not reliably uncorrelated in a selloff and it is not liquid enough to matter. Government bonds are the reliable, liquid, low-return mitigator, with a weaker cushion at low yields. Trend and managed futures is the higher-return option, but the hedge is less certain and strategy-dependent and liquidity is often low with lock-ups.

cues.signal: The investor proposes substituting investment-grade fixed income with private equity.
cues.implication: Two separate answers. On return, private equity lowers the risk of missing a long-term real target because investment-grade fixed income may not reach it. On risk, the considerations beyond volatility are illiquidity, the J-curve, vintage concentration, manager dispersion, embedded leverage, valuation lag, fee drag, due-diligence complexity and correlation rising in a crisis. A question asking for risks beyond volatility wants two of those with reasoning, not a restatement of standard deviation.

cues.signal: The investor commits its whole private equity target in a single year to reach the allocation sooner.
cues.implication: Over-commitment. Funds call roughly 25% of commitments a year over four years and run about ten years. Committed capital is a legal obligation, so the calls must be funded whatever the market does, and in a downturn managers may accelerate them while distributions slow. Recommend steady commitments across vintage years so maturing funds' distributions fund newer calls.

cues.signal: A severe-stress scenario asks which sources of liquidity deterioration apply to the endowment.
cues.implication: The three named drains: capital calls exceeding distributions, gates activating at hedge-fund and real-estate vehicles, and lagged private marks raising the private weight as liquid assets fall. Wider public-bond bid-ask spreads is the distractor, not one of the three.

cues.signal: A perpetual horizon, a 5% spending rule, a professional staff and a multi-billion pool, but the university draws about 30% of its operating budget from the endowment and the spending rate is smoothed, so it rises above 5% after a prolonged weak market.
cues.implication: Horizon, governance and scale all argue for a large private equity allocation. The operating-budget dependence and the countercyclical spending rate are the counterweight: that design stabilizes the university but worsens endowment liquidity exactly when calls exceed distributions, and a forced spending cut lands on 30% of the university's budget. Name the remedies, do not just name the check: stress-test spending plus capital calls under a severe market decline, raise the liquidity buffer, slow and pace new private commitments, and arrange a committed credit line or subscription facility.

cues.signal: A sovereign fund's mandate is stabilization, buffering the government budget against commodity-price or fiscal swings.
cues.implication: Rules large illiquid private stakes out: a stabilization mandate needs high liquidity and low risk. The same stake can be appropriate for a savings fund transferring wealth across generations. Judge the holding against the mandate, not in the abstract.

cues.signal: The investor is choosing between committing to external funds and taking direct stakes or co-investments.
cues.implication: Direct gives more control, avoids a layer of fees and allows tailored exposure, but it demands deal teams, board representation and in-house valuation capability, and it concentrates risk; the fund route outsources that at the cost of fees and control. Because exit is slow either way, the controls are ex-ante: diversify across companies, sectors, geographies and vintage years, take governance rights, set position limits, and hold liquid reserves.

cues.signal: A private equity holding is still carried at last-round cost a year after a down round.
cues.implication: Performance and Valuation under the Asset Manager Code. The remedy is a documented fair-value policy with independent input and a review calendar for Level 3 assets, not a disclosure footnote.

cues.signal: A trustee founded the private equity firm bidding for the mandate, and the portfolio manager advocating for it has a family tie to her.
cues.implication: Name the standards by actor. The trustee breaches Loyalty and Disclosure of Conflicts by pressing staff toward her own firm, and must disclose and recuse. The staff member and the CIO engage Independence and Objectivity and Disclosure of Conflicts, and common knowledge of the family tie is no substitute for explicit disclosure. A negotiated fee discount cures none of it, and presented performance that exceeds third-party databases must be investigated, which is a separate diligence failure.

cues.signal: The private program is described as established, mature and diversified across managers, strategies and vintages.
cues.implication: Those facts answer the concentration and start-up J-curve objections, so do not argue the program is too new. What is left to argue is short-term volatility against the board's stated long-term volatility range, and the liquidity budget.

_review.residualRisk: The previous pass aimed this note at the wrong claim. The 0.3 to 0.5 against 0.7 to 0.8 correlation range is the explicit grading key for elbe_society_the_elbe_society_essay_q5, one of only two essay stems in this key's grounding bundle, so it is the best-evidenced number in the entry and can be written down; its own hedge ('may be nearer') matches the key's wording. What actually needed flagging was the control-versus-influence cue, which had no support in the notes, the LOS or the question bank, and it has now been deleted. What is left in doubt: los[] is empty for this key, so nothing here is anchored to an official learning outcome statement; two of the quantitative illustrations are borrowed from other vehicle types and labelled as such (the 8% to 12-13% de-smoothing figure is a private real-asset fund, the 2-and-20 arithmetic is a hedge fund); the private equity fee convention stated against that arithmetic (carry on realized proceeds above a preferred return, management fee on committed capital) is general curriculum knowledge and is not in the bundled notes; and the GIPS money-weighted trigger list is deliberately wider than the notes, which teach the narrow conjunction. That is why confidence is medium rather than high.
